meaning: After a series of bad events, things end up in a terrible, ridiculous state.
connection: Verb dictionary form / ない-form + 始末だ; この・あの + 始末だ

senses.label: End up (so badly)
senses.meaning: After listing a chain of bad events, states the final bad outcome. Like “and in the end, ... even ...” or “it's come to the point where ...”. It shows the speaker's frustration, resignation, or blame. Only for negative outcomes.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form / ない-form / ている-form + 始末だ (often after 「〜し、〜し、挙げ句の果てに」, 「とうとう」, 「ついには」)
examples: My son never studies and just plays around, and now he's finally saying he'll quit school.
He kept coming in late, and in the end he even skipped work without notice.
Prices keep going up, and now I can't even afford enough vegetables.

senses.label: This is what it's come to
senses.meaning: 「この始末だ」 and 「あの始末だ」 point to the mess in front of you. Like “and look how it turned out”. Often used to scold others or mock oneself.
senses.connection: この／その／あの + 始末だ
examples: I warned you so many times, and look at this mess.
He said “leave it to me”, and look how that turned out.

notes: Only for bad outcomes; used for a good one it sounds sarcastic: ✕「毎日練習して、ついに優勝する始末だ」→ ○「毎日練習して、ついに優勝するに至った」.

It carries a clear tone of blame and disgust. Saying 「〜始末です」 about a superior's or client's behavior (e.g. 「部長は会議にも遅れる始末で」) amounts to scolding them to their face and is very rude; use it only for self-mockery or when commenting on a third party.

On its own, 「始末」 mostly means “dealing with, cleaning up”: 「火の始末をする」 is “to put a fire out properly”, 「始末書」 is “a written apology”, and 「始末が悪い」 is “hard to deal with”. Don't read all of these as “it has come to this”.
A string of events has to be laid out first, often with 「〜し、〜し、挙げ句の果てに／ついには〜始末だ」. A bare 「彼は会社をやめる始末だ」 with no lead-up sounds abrupt.

daily.title: Complaining about a child
daily.description: A mother tells a friend her child is getting out of hand.
daily.example: Lately he just talks back, and yesterday he even said he'd run away from home.

daily.title: Laughing at a failed diet
daily.description: Joking with a friend about not sticking to it.
daily.example: I started a diet, and here I am eating ramen in the middle of the night.

daily.title: Reacting to the news
daily.description: Commenting on a news story.
daily.example: The response was slow, and in the end people even died.

work.title: Reviewing a failed project
work.description: Looking back in a meeting at how a project got worse step by step.
work.example: The specs kept changing, and in the end we couldn't even meet the deadline.

work.title: Reporting a corporate scandal
work.description: News commentary on a company's poor response.
work.example: The company kept changing its explanation, and in the end it even canceled the press conference.

etymology: 「始末」 comes from Chinese: 「始」 (beginning) and 「末」 (end) mean the whole course of events, and so the outcome. 「始末だ」 means “the outcome is ...”, and later came to be used only for bad outcomes.

similar.title: 〜あげく
similar.explanation: Both describe a bad ending after a series of troubles. 「〜あげく」 follows the process (verb た-form / noun + の + あげく) and then the result comes after it. 「〜始末だ」 sits at the end of the sentence and states the outcome directly, with the process told separately, and its tone of blame is stronger. Compare 「迷ったあげく、買わなかった」, which is just narration, with 「遊んでばかりで、ついには退学する始末だ」, which carries clear displeasure.

similar.title: 〜末(に)
similar.explanation: 「〜末に」 also means “after ..., finally”, but the result can be good or bad, and it is mostly used for a conclusion reached after long thought or effort (「悩んだ末に決めた」). 「〜始末だ」 is only for bad results and carries the speaker's displeasure. Both contain 「末」 (end).

similar.title: 〜に至る／〜に至って
similar.explanation: 「〜に至る」 objectively states that things finally developed to some major point (「死者を出すに至った」), and is common in news and reports. 「〜始末だ」 is the speaker's subjective complaint, “it has actually come to this”, and is much more emotional.

similar.title: 〜結果
similar.explanation: 「〜結果」 neutrally states “as a result of ...”, good or bad, with no emotion. 「〜始末だ」 names only bad endings and carries blame or resignation.

formation: 「始末」 is made of 「始」 (beginning) and 「末」 (end). It originally meant the whole course of a matter from start to finish, and from there “the final outcome”. With the copula 「だ」 at the end, it literally says “the outcome (of it all) is ...”. Because the outcome is named last, the earlier events have to be told first, which gives the pattern “lay out the process, then reveal the result”. In Japanese, 「始末」 is also tied to “cleaning up a mess” (「後始末」, 「始末書」), so the outcome of 「〜始末だ」 is almost always a mess that needs cleaning up, with a note of dissatisfaction or resignation. 「この始末だ」 simply points at the outcome in front of you with a demonstrative: “and this is how it turned out”.

meaning: You want to do something but have no way or means to do it; there's nothing you can do.
connection: Verb dictionary form + すべがない／すべもない (written 「術」 in kanji)

senses.label: No way to
senses.meaning: There's no method or means to do what you want. Like “there's no way to ...” or “can't possibly ...”. More literary than 「方法がない」, with a sense of helplessness.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + すべがない／すべはない／すべがなかった (common: 知る・伝える・防ぐ・確かめる)
examples: There's no way to know where he is now.
I had no way to express how I felt.
There's no way to confirm whether that story is true.

senses.label: Helpless
senses.meaning: 「なす術もない」 and 「なす術もなく」 are set phrases: completely helpless in the face of a disaster, a strong opponent, and so on. 「も」 is stronger than 「が」.
senses.connection: なす + 術もない／術もなく
examples: People were helpless before the tsunami.
Up against a powerhouse team, we lost without putting up a fight.

notes: 「術」 is read 「すべ」 here; reading it 「じゅつ」 is a common mistake. This reading is outside the 「常用漢字」 list, so newspapers and textbooks often write it in kana as 「すべ」.

Its connection is exactly the opposite of 「〜ようがない」, so they are easily confused. 「〜ようがない」 attaches to the stem of the ます-form (「知りようがない」), while 「〜すべがない」 attaches to the dictionary form: ✕「知りすべがない」→ ○「知るすべがない」.
It is literary and heavy in tone, as if one is cornered with no way out. In everyday conversation, or when explaining something to a client, 「方法がありません」 or 「〜しようがありません」 sounds more natural.

daily.title: Lost touch with an old friend
daily.description: Talking to family about a friend from years ago.
daily.example: He moved away, and now I have no way to contact him.

daily.title: Watching disaster news
daily.description: Reacting to a flood report.
daily.example: Houses were swept away by the muddy water, and the residents were helpless.

work.title: Explaining a stalled investigation
work.description: Reporting to a boss that information can't be verified.
work.example: No records remain, so there's no way to confirm what the situation was at the time.

work.title: Sports news
work.description: Reporting a one-sided match.
work.example: Japan was pinned back the whole game and lost helplessly.

etymology: 「すべ」 (術) is a native Japanese word meaning “means, method”. Old Japanese already had phrases like 「せむすべなし」 (nothing to be done). Today it survives mainly in set expressions like 「〜すべがない」 and 「なす術もない」.

similar.title: 〜ようがない
similar.explanation: The closest in meaning; both say “there is no way to do it”. 「〜ようがない」 attaches to the stem of the ます-form (「知りようがない」) and is common in both speech and writing, while 「〜すべがない」 attaches to the dictionary form (「知るすべがない」) and is more formal and literary.

similar.title: 〜べくもない
similar.explanation: 「〜べくもない」 stresses “judging from the situation, it is simply impossible” (「勝つべくもない」), a judgment about possibility. 「〜すべがない」 stresses “no means or route can be found”. Both are very formal.

similar.title: 〜どうにも〜ない／〜てもどうにもならない
similar.explanation: 「どうにも〜ない」 and 「どうにもならない」 are spoken ways of saying “there's just nothing I can do”, with a tone of frustration and resignation. 「〜すべがない」 is a calm, written-style statement, mostly found in prose.

formation: 「すべ」 is a native Japanese noun meaning “means, way” (written with the borrowed kanji 「術」). The dictionary form of a verb modifies it directly, so 「知るすべ」 is “a way to find out”, and 「が＋ない」 says that such a way does not exist. Literally it is “there is no way to ...”, and the stress is on the lack of a “means”: it is not that you don't want to, but that you can't find a route. Changing 「が」 to 「も」 (「なす術もない」) gives “not even a way”, a more complete denial, and that became the fixed phrase for “completely helpless”. 「すべ」 itself is an archaic word, which gives the whole phrase its literary flavor.

meaning: 「ただ」 and 「のみ」 work together to strongly limit the scope: “only ...”, “nothing but ...”.
connection: ただ + noun / verb dictionary form + のみ（だ）

senses.label: All one can do is
senses.meaning: There's nothing else to do but this. Like “all I can do is ...” or “the only thing left is to ...”. Often sounds determined or resigned.
senses.connection: ただ + verb dictionary form + のみだ／のみです (common: 待つ・祈る・進む・努力する)
examples: I've done everything I can. All that's left is to wait for the results.
All we can do is move forward.
Right now, all I can do is pray that everyone is safe.

senses.label: Only this
senses.meaning: Limits a noun or number: “just this, nothing more”. Like “only ...” or “just ...”. More formal than 「だけ」.
senses.connection: ただ + noun / number + のみ
examples: Only one person passed the exam.
The only thing on his mind is winning.

notes: It differs from 「ただ〜のみならず」 only by 「ならず」, yet the meaning is completely different: 「ただ祈るのみだ」 is “all I can do is pray”, while 「ただ祈るのみならず」 is “not only pray (but also ...)”.
「のみ」 follows the dictionary form of a verb or a noun, not the ます-form, and no 「だ」 is added after a noun: ✕「ただ待ちますのみです」→ ○「ただ待つのみです」.
The tone is solemn and resolute, suited to speeches and statements of determination. In casual chat, 「ただ待つのみだ」 sounds exaggerated and put-on; in speech use 「待つしかない」 or 「待つだけだ」.
The 「ただ」 here means “only, merely”. It is not the 「ただ」 meaning “free of charge”, nor the sentence-initial 「ただ、〜」 meaning “however, but”.

daily.title: After an exam
daily.description: A student tells a friend how they feel.
daily.example: It's over now, so all I can do is pray I passed.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: The hero makes up his mind.
daily.example: I have no doubts. I will simply walk my own path.

work.title: Pre-game interview
work.description: An athlete speaks to reporters.
work.example: We're fully prepared. All that's left is to give it everything we've got.

work.title: Company speech
work.description: The president speaks at a year-end event.
work.example: All we can do is keep working with integrity.

etymology: 「ただ」 (唯・只) is an adverb meaning “only”. 「のみ」 is often said to come from old 「の＋身」, meaning “just”. Both are limiting words, and stacking them adds emphasis.

similar.title: 〜のみ
similar.explanation: Same origin. 「のみ」 alone is already the written-style “only”; adding 「ただ」 in front makes a matching frame and strengthens the exclusiveness, and it is often used for resolve (「ただ待つのみ」).

similar.title: 〜だけ
similar.explanation: 「ただ〜だけ」 is the spoken counterpart with basically the same meaning; 「ただ〜のみ」 is more formal and solemn, suited to speeches and writing.

similar.title: 〜までだ／〜までのことだ
similar.explanation: 「〜までだ」 also means “there is nothing but ...” (「だめならやり直すまでだ」), but with a brisk “at worst I'll just ..., no big deal” tone. 「ただ〜のみ」 solemnly stresses that there is nothing else to do.

similar.title: 〜ただ〜のみならず
similar.explanation: Same origin and also built from 「ただ」 and 「のみ」, but with 「ならず」 added the meaning becomes “not only ... but also ...”. The forms differ by just two characters, which makes it a common distractor on tests.

formation: It is built by sandwiching the middle element between the limiting adverb 「ただ」 (only) and the literary limiting particle 「のみ」. 「ただ」 at the front announces “there will be just one thing”, and 「のみ」 at the end draws the boundary again; the same “only” is said twice, so the limitation is doubled and strongly exclusive. When the middle is a verb (「祈る」, 「待つ」), it means “there is nothing to do except this”, which naturally brings out a tone of resolve or of leaving things to fate (“all that remains is to ...”). When the middle is a noun or a quantity (「一人」), it simply means “just ...”. 「のみ」 itself is literary, so the whole phrase sounds dignified.

meaning: Not limited to the first item; it extends to the second as well. Like “not just ... (but also ...)”.
connection: ただ + noun / plain form + のみならず

senses.label: Not only this thing
senses.meaning: A problem, effect, etc. isn't limited to the first item but covers a wider range. Like “not just ..., but also ...”. More formal and solemn than 「〜だけでなく」. The second part often has 「も」, 「まで」, or 「全体」.
senses.connection: ただ + noun + のみならず、〜も (common: 日本・個人・国内・若者)
examples: Environmental problems are not just one country's issue, but a challenge for the whole world.
This law will have a big impact not only on companies but also on individuals.

senses.label: Not only did ...
senses.meaning: After a verb or adjective: it's not only this fact, there's something more. Often used to praise or to stress how serious something is. A slightly less stiff version is 「ただ〜のみでなく」.
senses.connection: ただ + verb / い-adjective plain form, or な-adjective + である + のみならず; ただ〜のみでなく
examples: He's not only a great singer, he's also a talented composer.
That remark not only hurt the other person, it also damaged the company's reputation.
Reading doesn't just give you knowledge; it also enriches your heart.

notes: It differs from 「ただ〜のみ」 (“only”) only by 「ならず」, yet the meaning is completely different: 「ただ勝つのみだ」 is “I only seek victory”, while 「ただ勝つのみならず」 is “not only win (but also ...)”.
It must be followed by a “wider scope”, often echoed with 「も」 or 「まで」; the first half alone is incomplete: ✕「この問題はただ日本のみならず。」→ ○「この問題はただ日本のみならず、世界の問題でもある。」
Nouns attach directly, with no 「だ」; for な-adjectives use 「であるのみならず」: ✕「ただ便利だのみならず」→ ○「ただ便利であるのみならず」.
It is very formal and solemn; in everyday conversation it sounds exaggerated. In speech say 「〜だけじゃなくて」.

daily.title: News commentary
daily.description: A commentator talks about a social issue.
daily.example: The falling birthrate is serious not only in rural areas but in cities too.

daily.title: Reading a biography
daily.description: A biography describes someone's achievements.
daily.example: He made his name not only as a doctor but also as a writer.

work.title: Academic paper
work.description: A paper explains the value of its research.
work.example: This study is significant not only in theory but also in practice.

work.title: Corporate speech
work.description: A president stresses the company's social responsibility.
work.example: We must not only pursue profit but also contribute to society.

etymology: 「のみならず」 is made of the limiting particle 「のみ」 + 「ならず」, the negative of the classical copula 「なり」, literally “not being only ...”. The adverb 「ただ」 (唯) adds emphasis. It's a formal style that comes from reading classical Chinese texts in Japanese.

similar.title: 〜のみならず
similar.explanation: Same origin and same meaning. Adding 「ただ」 strengthens the emphasis on “not limited to this” and makes it more solemn; it is common in speeches and papers.

similar.title: 〜ひとり〜のみならず
similar.explanation: Almost the same meaning and often interchangeable. 「ひとり」 originally means “just one”, so it is mostly used for “not only one person, one country or one region”. 「ただ」 has a wider range and can also attach to verbs and adjectives.

similar.title: 〜にとどまらず
similar.explanation: 「〜にとどまらず」 stresses “it did not stop within a certain range but spread out”, and the first item is usually a range or field (「国内にとどまらず」). 「ただ〜のみならず」 is a plain addition, “not only ... but also ...”, with a stronger written flavor.

similar.title: 〜ばかりでなく
similar.explanation: 「〜ばかりでなく」 is “not only ... but also ...” and works in both speech and writing. 「ただ〜のみならず」 means the same but is the most formal and solemn.

formation: It consists of three parts: the adverb 「ただ」 (only), the limiting particle 「のみ」, and 「ならず」. 「ならず」 is the negative of the classical copula 「なり」, equivalent to modern 「ではなく」, so 「のみならず」 literally means “it is not only ...”. First 「ただ〜のみ」 limits the range to the first item, then 「ならず」 negates that limit, so the range opens up and extends to the second item: “not only ... but also ...”. The opening 「ただ」 strengthens the premise “only the first item”, so the contrast of “the range is actually wider” stands out more, which is why it is often used to stress how broad a problem or influence is. The whole phrase has a 漢文訓読 (classical Chinese reading) style and a strongly written flavor.

meaning: Something is serious: it can't be settled with just a certain level of response or attitude, and heavier consequences or responsibility will follow.
connection: Noun / plain form + ではすまない／ではすまされない

senses.label: Won't be enough
senses.meaning: The first item (an apology, a joke, something minor) won't settle the matter. Like “... won't cut it” or “it's not something you can settle with just ...”. Suggests more serious consequences.
senses.connection: Noun + では済まない (common: 冗談・謝罪・ごめん・笑い事); verb dictionary form + だけでは済まない
examples: This is no longer a problem you can laugh off.
With damage this widespread, an apology alone probably won't be enough.
If you make another mistake, you won't get off with a warning.

senses.label: Can't be excused
senses.meaning: 「〜ではすまされない」 uses the passive to stress that society or others won't let it end with just ... . Often used when holding someone responsible. 「知らなかったではすまされない」 is a common phrase.
senses.connection: Plain form (quoted) / noun + では済まされない
examples: “I didn't know” is no excuse.
Misconduct by public officials can't be dismissed as a personal matter.

notes: It is the exact opposite of the affirmative 「〜で済む」: 「謝って済む問題」 is “a problem that can be settled by apologizing”, while 「謝るだけでは済まない問題」 is “a problem that can't be settled by an apology alone”.

It is easily confused with 「〜ずにはすまない／ないではすまない」 (“I can't get away without ...”): 「謝らないでは済まない」 means “I have to apologize”, while 「謝るだけでは済まない」 means “an apology alone isn't enough”. Check whether what comes before is 「ない」 or a noun / 「だけ」.
A verb can't attach directly; add 「だけ」 or turn it into a noun: ✕「謝るでは済まない」→ ○「謝るだけでは済まない」「謝罪では済まない」.

The tone is stern, with a sense of warning and assigning blame. Saying 「これは〜では済まされませんよ」 to a client or superior amounts to a threat and is very rude. When apologizing, you can turn it on yourself: 「お詫びだけで済むこととは思っておりません」.

daily.title: Parent scolding a child
daily.description: The child broke a neighbor's window.
daily.example: You broke someone's window. “Sorry” isn't going to cut it.

daily.title: Reacting to the news
daily.description: Commenting on a traffic accident report.
daily.example: Drunk driving can't be excused as a careless mistake.

work.title: Boss warning a subordinate
work.description: The subordinate made a serious error in a contract.
work.example: A mistake in the contract amount won't be settled with a written apology.

work.title: Corporate crisis response
work.description: The company discusses a data leak.
work.example: A leak of personal information is not something an apology alone can settle.

etymology: 「すむ」 (済む) originally means “to end, to be settled”. 「〜で済む」 is “settled with ...”; in the negative it becomes 「〜では済まない」, and the passive 「済まされない」 stresses that others won't allow it.

similar.title: 〜て済む・〜ずに済む
similar.explanation: Same origin (both from 「済む」) and the affirmative counterpart of this pattern: 「軽いけがで済んだ」 is “it ended with only a minor injury”, with a sense of relief. 「〜ではすまない」 is its negation, saying the cost won't be that small.

similar.title: 〜ずにはすまない／〜ないではすまない
similar.explanation: Same origin and similar in form, so the easiest to confuse. 「〜ずにはすまない」 attaches to the negative form of a verb and means “(out of duty or social expectation) I can't not do ...”, while 「〜ではすまない」 attaches to a noun or 「〜だけ」 and means “... alone won't settle it”.

formation: It is built from the case particle 「で」 (means or extent: “with ...”), the topic particle 「は」, and the negative 「済まない」 of the verb 「済む」 (to be settled, to be finished). 「〜で済む」 means “it can be settled with ...”, implying that the cost is small. Adding 「は」 lifts the first item out for contrast, and negating it gives “it can't be settled with ... alone”, hinting that a bigger price has to be paid. In the passive 「済まされない」, the one who “settles” (「済ます」, to treat as finished) becomes the people around you or society: “(others) won't let you off with just ...”. That is why it is mostly used to hold someone responsible or to give a warning.

meaning: Because of one's face, position, or what one has already said or done, one has to (or can't) act a certain way.
connection: Noun + の / verb plain form + 手前

senses.label: Having said that
senses.meaning: After something you've already said or done: to save face, you can't back out now. Like “since I already ...” or “having said so ...”. Often followed by 「〜わけにはいかない」 or 「〜しかない」.
senses.connection: Verb た-form + 手前 (common: 言った・約束した・引き受けた・大口をたたいた)
examples: Since I promised I'd definitely go, I can't back out now.
I volunteered for it myself, so I can't quit halfway.

senses.label: In front of
senses.meaning: After a person or a situation: in front of others, you must watch what you say or do. Like “in front of ...” or “out of regard for ...”.
senses.connection: Noun + の手前; verb ている-form + 手前
examples: We try not to argue in front of the kids.
With my team watching, I couldn't show any weakness.

notes: 「手前」 is also the humble “our side” in 「手前ども」 (said by shopkeepers to customers), and the rude slang 「てめえ」 (“you bastard”) comes from 「てまえ」. Never address someone as 「手前」 or 「てめえ」; it is extremely rude.

As an ordinary noun, 「手前」 means “the near side, the position closer to you”: 「駅の手前で止まる」 is “stop just before the station”. When you see 「名詞＋の手前」, first decide whether it is a position or “out of regard for ...'s face”.

The second half is mostly “can't ... / have no choice but to ...”, expressing being bound by face or position; it is unnatural with something positive and voluntary: ✕「約束した手前、喜んで行く」→ ○「約束した手前、行かないわけにはいかない」.

daily.title: Going reluctantly
daily.description: You told a friend you'd go but now don't want to.
daily.example: Well, I said I'd go, so I guess I have to.

daily.title: In front of the kids
daily.description: A parent explains why they don't smoke at home.
daily.example: For the kids' sake, I decided to quit smoking.

work.title: Project leader
work.description: Hitting trouble after volunteering.
work.example: I raised my hand for this, so I can't complain.

work.title: Being mindful of clients
work.description: Handling a problem with a client present.
work.example: With the client there, I didn't say anything at the time.

etymology: 「手前」 originally means “at hand, right in front”, the area near you. It came to mean “in front of someone's eyes”, and then “one's face or standing in front of others”.

similar.title: 〜以上(は)
similar.explanation: Both can be rendered “since ..., then ...”. 「〜以上は」 stresses logical necessity and responsibility (「契約した以上は守るべきだ」); 「〜手前」 stresses regard for face and for other people's eyes, with a feeling of being in a bind.

similar.title: 〜からには
similar.explanation: 「〜からには」 mostly expresses a positive resolve (“since ..., I'll see it through”), and the second half is often will or duty. 「〜手前」 mostly expresses being forced into something with no way back.

similar.title: 〜上は
similar.explanation: 「〜上は」 is formal and solemn: “since a decision has been made or things have come to this, I must take the corresponding responsibility”. 「〜手前」 is more colloquial and focuses on face in human relationships.

formation: 「手前」 is made of 「手」 (hand) and 「前」 (front), originally “the space in front of one's hand”, that is, the spot closest to you, right before your eyes. From “before one's eyes” it came to mean “in front of someone, in someone's presence”, and then “one's face or standing before others”. So 「子供の手前」 is “in front of the child (so I have to watch how I look)”, and 「約束した手前」 treats your own words as something laid out in plain view of everyone: since the words are already out there, it is hard to take them back. Because the core idea is “being watched”, the second half is naturally about things like “I have to ...” or “it would be awkward to ...”, being bound by one's position.

meaning: After a word for a period of time, stresses that a state continued throughout that long period.
connection: Noun for a period + というもの

senses.label: For the whole ...
senses.meaning: Stresses “for this long”, a state continued the whole time. Like “for the past ...” or “all this ...”. The speaker feels the time was long and sounds moved or weary. Often preceded by 「この」 or 「ここ」.
senses.connection: (この／ここ) + period noun + というもの (common: 一週間・一か月・数年・十年)
examples: I've barely slept this whole past week.
For the past few years, I haven't heard a thing from him.
The three months since I was hospitalized felt really long.

notes: The second half must be a continuing state or a repeated situation that spans the whole period, not a one-time action: ✕「この一週間というもの、引っ越しをした」→ ○「この一週間というもの、引っ越しの準備に追われていた」.
It carries a feeling of “all this long time ...”; don't use it for a plain statement of a period: ✕「この三日間というもの、会議は三回あった」→ ○「この三日間、会議は三回あった」.

It looks the same as 「〜というものだ」 (“that's how it should be”) but means something completely different: 「それが親というものだ」 is “that's what being a parent is”. First check whether what precedes is a word for a period of time.

daily.title: Complaining to a friend
daily.description: You've been busy for a while.
daily.example: This whole past month, I haven't had a single day off.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A character's longing is described.
daily.example: In all these ten years, not a day has gone by that I haven't thought of her.

work.title: News report
work.description: Reporting days of unusual weather.
work.example: For the past week, record-breaking heat has continued across the country.

work.title: Explaining background in a meeting
work.description: Explaining a long sales slump.
work.example: For the past six months, sales have remained sluggish.

etymology: 「というもの」 is quoting 「と言う」 + the formal noun 「もの」, originally “the thing called ...”. After a period word, it treats that stretch of time as one whole and stresses how long it was.

similar.title: 〜てからというもの
similar.explanation: Same origin and same structure. 「〜てからというもの」 takes some event as the starting point and means “ever since ..., things have been different”; 「期間＋というもの」 only stresses the length of a period.

similar.title: 〜にわたって
similar.explanation: Both relate to a span of time. 「〜にわたって」 objectively describes how far a period or range extends (「三日間にわたって会議が行われた」), and the second half can be an event; 「〜というもの」 carries the feeling of “all this long time, continuously ...”, and the second half is a continuing state.

similar.title: 〜というものだ
similar.explanation: Same origin (both built from 「という＋もの」) but a different meaning: 「〜というものだ」 is a judgment, “so-called ... is like this, that's how it should be”, while this pattern stresses a period. They look the same, so check whether what comes before is a word for a period of time.

formation: It is made of the quotative 「と言う」 and the formal noun 「もの」, so 「〜というもの」 literally means “this thing called ...”. Putting a period of time (「この一週間」) into it picks that period out as one complete “thing” and presents it: “this week — this whole stretch of time”. Picking it out like this already carries emphasis and emotion, hinting that the time was long and out of the ordinary. Since the whole period is viewed as one whole, the second half has to be a continuing state that runs through the entire period.

meaning: Gives two typical examples to say it applies everywhere, without distinction. Like “whether it's ... or ..., everywhere (always) ...”.
connection: Noun A + といわず、noun B + といわず

senses.label: Both A and B, everywhere
senses.meaning: Gives two examples of the same kind to say it's not just them; the whole thing is in that state. Like “both ... and ..., all over”. Often describes something surprising or unpleasant.
senses.connection: Noun A + といわず + noun B + といわず (common: 顔・手, 昼・夜, 家の中・外)
examples: The kids were covered in mud, face, hands, everything.
Day and night, the construction noise is loud.
Inside the trains and in the stations, everywhere was packed with people.

senses.label: Don't wait until
senses.meaning: 「〜といわず」 alone, after a time word: “don't wait until ...; (do it) now”. Often paired with 「今すぐ」 or 「今日にでも」 to urge quick action.
senses.connection: Time noun + といわず (common: 明日・来週・来年)
examples: Don't wait until tomorrow. You should go to the hospital today.
Why wait until next year? Let's start this year.

notes: If A and B are concrete things of the same category (body parts, places, times), it means “all, everywhere”; words of different kinds can't be paired: ✕「顔といわず性格といわず」→ ○「顔といわず手といわず」.
It looks similar to 「〜といい〜といい」: 「味といい値段といい、満足だ」 evaluates from several aspects, while 「顔といわず手といわず泥だらけだ」 describes the overall state without any evaluative angle.
The standalone 「明日と言わず今日にでも」 means “don't wait until tomorrow, do it even today”, and the second half is mostly a persuasion; this differs from “whether A or B”.
The ordinary negative 「言わず」 is also very common: 「何も言わず出て行った」 is “left without saying a word”, which is not this pattern.

daily.title: Describing a naughty cat
daily.description: Telling a friend about your cat.
daily.example: Our cat shreds everything with its claws, the sofa, the curtains, you name it.

daily.title: Urging a friend to see a doctor
daily.description: Your friend feels ill but keeps putting it off.
daily.example: Don't wait for the weekend. Go get checked today.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A novel describes the hero's busy life.
daily.example: Holidays or weekdays, he was absorbed in his research.

work.title: Disaster news
work.description: Reporting the scene after a typhoon.
work.example: Roads and fields alike are all under water.

work.title: Reporting frequent failures
work.description: Telling the boss about system problems.
work.example: Errors are occurring morning and night.

etymology: Made of the quoting particle 「と」 + 「言わず」, the classical negative of 「言う」. Literally “without calling it A, without calling it B”, i.e. “whether you call it A or B”, which came to mean “A and B alike, everything”.

similar.title: 〜といい〜といい
similar.explanation: Similar in form; both give two examples. 「〜といい〜といい」 evaluates a person or thing from several aspects (praise or criticism), while 「〜といわず〜といわず」 stresses that the whole range is in some state, without an evaluative angle.

similar.title: 〜という（emphasizing all / quantity）
similar.explanation: 「NというN」 (「窓という窓」) also means “every single ..., without exception” and is very close in meaning, but it repeats the same noun, while 「〜といわず〜といわず」 gives two different representative examples.

similar.title: 〜を問わず
similar.explanation: 「〜を問わず」 is usually preceded by paired or contrasting concepts such as “men and women, age, day and night” and means “regardless of”; it is common in rules and advertisements. 「〜といわず〜といわず」 follows concrete things and describes an actual state in front of you.

similar.title: 〜に限らず
similar.explanation: 「〜に限らず」 gives only one example and means “not limited to ...”, with the second half mostly “... too”; 「〜といわず〜といわず」 gives two examples and means “all over”.

formation: It is built from the quotative particle 「と」 and 「言わず」, the literary negative form of 「言う」. 「Aと言わず」 literally means “without saying it is A”, that is, “without singling out A”. When both examples A and B of the same kind are “not singled out”, it becomes “whether A or B, without distinction”, which extends to the whole range: “everywhere, all over”. So A and B are only representatives, and the real focus is “everything”. When used alone with a time word, 「〜と言わず」 turns “not saying tomorrow” into “no need to wait until tomorrow (do it now)”.

meaning: Written style: “even ...”, “even if ...”. Usually followed by a negative or discouraging result.
connection: Noun + とて; verb た-form + とて; 〜からとて

senses.label: Even someone
senses.meaning: Names a person or thing and says even it is no exception. Like “even ...” or “... is no different”. Stiffer and more formal than 「〜でも」. Common in 「私とて」 and 「誰とて」.
senses.connection: Noun + とて (common: 私・彼・親・大人・プロ・誰)
examples: Even I feel just as frustrated as everyone else.
Even veteran doctors make mistakes sometimes.
There's no one, whoever they are, who doesn't fear death.

senses.label: Even if you did
senses.meaning: Even if you do the first thing, you won't get the result you want. Like “even if ..., (it's no use)”. The second part is usually negative or futile, often with 「いくら」 or 「今さら」.
senses.connection: Verb た-form + とて
examples: Even if you apologize now, you probably won't be forgiven.
No matter how much we hurry, we won't make it now.
Crying won't change anything.

senses.label: Just because
senses.meaning: 「〜からとて」 equals 「〜からといって」: “just because ... doesn't mean ...”. The second part is usually negative or a prohibition. It's an old-fashioned, literary form.
senses.connection: Plain form + からとて
examples: You shouldn't spoil children just because they're children.
Being busy doesn't mean it's OK to break promises.

notes: A verb must be in the た-form: ✕「謝るとて、許してもらえない」→ ○「謝ったとて、許してもらえない」.
It differs from 「〜こととて」 (“because ...”): 「慣れぬこととて、失礼しました」 is “since I'm not used to it, please excuse my rudeness”, not “even if I'm not used to it”.
It is literary and archaic, and in everyday conversation it sounds affected. In speech use 「〜だって」, 「〜たって」, or 「〜からといって」 respectively.
The 「とて」 in 「とても」 (very) and 「とてつもない」 has nothing to do with this pattern.

daily.title: Comforting a friend
daily.description: Your friend failed an exam; you've failed before too.
daily.example: I've failed plenty of times myself, you know.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A character's inner monologue.
daily.example: Even if I regret it now, she won't come back.

work.title: News commentary
work.description: Commenting that even big companies face crises.
work.example: Even big companies can't survive if they can't adapt to change.

work.title: Formal speech
work.description: A manager stresses the rules at a meeting.
work.example: Being an executive doesn't make you an exception to the rules.

etymology: 「とて」 is the quoting particle 「と」 + the conjunctive particle 「て」, originally meaning 「と言って」 or 「と思って」. It later took on a concessive meaning, “even if you say ...”. In classical Japanese, 「〜とて」 could also show purpose or reason.

similar.title: 〜といえども
similar.explanation: Both mean “even if it's ...”. 「〜といえども」 is more formal and stiff, common in law, speeches and news (「子供といえども容赦しない」); 「〜とて」 carries a little more emotion and is common in literature and self-statements (「私とて」).

similar.title: 〜たところで
similar.explanation: Almost the same as 「た形＋とて」; both mean “even if you do it, it's no use”. 「〜たところで」 is common in both speech and writing, while 「〜たとて」 is an archaic written form.

similar.title: 〜からといって
similar.explanation: 「〜からとて」 is the literary, archaic form of 「〜からといって」 with the same meaning; both mean “you can't ... just because ...”, and the second half is mostly negative.

similar.title: 〜こととて
similar.explanation: Same origin (both contain 「とて」) but a different meaning: 「〜こととて」 expresses a reason, “because it is ..., (please excuse me)”, and is mostly used in apologies; 「〜とて」 is concessive, “even if ...”.

formation: It is built from the quotative particle 「と」 and the conjunctive particle 「て」, originally an abbreviation of 「と言って」 or 「と思って」, meaning “saying that ... and ...”. Used concessively, 「Aとて」 means “even if you say it is A, ...”: it first puts A forward as a condition, then overturns the expectation about it in the second half. After a noun (「私とて」) it means “even I”, stressing “I'm no exception”. After the た-form of a verb (「謝ったとて」) it means “even if I did apologize”, and the second half gives the futile result “it doesn't help”. 「からとて」 means “even if it's because ...”, equal to 「からといって」. Since it keeps the abbreviated form of classical Japanese, the whole phrase has a literary, archaic feel.

meaning: Shows a sudden, complete change compared with how things were before.
connection: Noun + とはうってかわって (打って変わって)

senses.label: Completely different from
senses.meaning: Things have totally changed compared with before. Like “in sharp contrast to ...” or “unlike ...”. Often used for sudden changes in weather, attitude, mood, or situation. Often preceded by 「昨日」, 「以前」, 「前回」.
senses.connection: Noun + とは打って変わって (common: 昨日・以前・前半・普段)
examples: Unlike yesterday, it's been a beautiful day since this morning.
He's a changed man and is working hard now.
In the second half, in sharp contrast to the first, Japan went on the attack.

senses.label: Transformed
senses.meaning: 「打って変わった + noun」 modifies a noun: “a totally changed ...”. 「打って変わり」 is used to link clauses. Both stress how fast and how big the change is.
senses.connection: 打って変わった + noun; 打って変わり、〜
examples: After being scolded, he sat there, suddenly very quiet.
At night the town was transformed, wrapped in silence.

notes: It compares the before and after of the same thing; it can't be used to compare two different things: ✕「兄とは打って変わって、弟は静かだ」→ ○「兄にひきかえ、弟は静かだ」.
It expresses a sudden, complete change, not a slow gradual one: ✕「少しずつ打って変わってきた」→ ○「少しずつ変わってきた」.
The comparison point takes 「とは」, not 「より」: ✕「昨日より打って変わって」→ ○「昨日とは打って変わって」. 「打って」 only adds emphasis and has nothing to do with “hitting”.

daily.title: Talking about the weather
daily.description: The day after a heavy storm, it cleared up.
daily.example: What a change from yesterday's downpour. It's totally clear.

daily.title: A friend has changed
daily.description: A friend changed after starting a relationship.
daily.example: Since he got a girlfriend, he's become so much more cheerful than before.

work.title: Stock market news
work.description: The market suddenly turned around.
work.example: In contrast to the previous day, stock prices rose sharply.

work.title: Evaluating in a meeting
work.description: Assessing the change a new manager brought.
work.example: Since the new structure began, the workplace has a completely different atmosphere.

etymology: 「打って変わる」 is 「打つ」 + 「変わる」. Here 「打つ」 is an intensifying prefix meaning “suddenly, completely”, so the whole means “to change completely all at once”.

similar.title: 〜にひきかえ
similar.explanation: Both express contrast. 「〜にひきかえ」 compares two different things (「兄にひきかえ、弟は…」) and is often evaluative; 「〜とはうってかわって」 compares the before and after of the same thing.

similar.title: 〜に対して
similar.explanation: The contrastive use of 「〜に対して」 objectively sets two things side by side (「兄が活発なのに対して、弟は静かだ」); 「〜とはうってかわって」 stresses that the same thing changed drastically, as if it were a different one.

formation: It is made of 「〜とは」 plus 「打って変わって」. The 「打つ」 in 「打って変わる」 is an intensifying element (generally thought to be like the 「打ち」 in 「打ち明ける」 and 「打ち消す」), meaning “all at once, thoroughly”, and followed by 「変わる」 it means “changed completely all at once”. The 「とは」 in front is the 「と」 that marks the thing compared (as in 「Aと違う」) plus the topic particle 「は」, lifting the “earlier state” out as the baseline for comparison. The whole phrase means “compared with ..., it changed completely all at once”. Since it compares the before and after of the same thing, words for a past state such as 「昨日」, 「以前」 or 「前半」 often appear in front.

meaning: Expresses a minimal hope, “even just a little”; after a question word, it means “any ... at all”.
connection: Noun/adverb of small amount + なりとも; question word + なりと（も）

senses.label: Even a little
senses.meaning: Names a bare minimum: “even just this much would be good”. Like “even a little” or “at least somewhat”. The second part is usually a wish, intention, or request.
senses.connection: 少し・多少・わずか・一目・一日 etc. + なりとも
examples: I'd be glad if I can be of even a little help to you all.
I want to see my mother, even if only for a moment.
I want to help the disaster area, even if only a little.

senses.label: Anything at all
senses.meaning: After a question word: “any ... is fine”. Like “anything at all” or “anywhere”. 「何なりと」 is common in customer service.
senses.connection: 何・誰・どこへ + なりと（も）
examples: If you need anything, please don't hesitate to ask.
Go wherever you like.

notes: It is preceded by a word for a “small amount” (「少し」, 「一目」, 「多少」, 「微力」), and the second half is a wish or request; it can't take large amounts: ✕「たくさんなりとも」→ ○「少しなりとも」.

It looks like 「〜たりとも」 but they can't be swapped: 「一円たりとも無駄にできない」 is “can't waste even one yen” (followed by a negative), while 「少しなりとも役に立ちたい」 is “I'd like to be of use, even if only a little” (followed by a wish).
It is formal and solemn, often used in speeches and letters (「微力なりともお力になれれば」); in everyday speech use 「少しでも」 or 「せめて〜でも」.

daily.title: Visiting someone in hospital
daily.description: You want to visit a friend in hospital.
daily.example: Even if it's just for a short time, I want to go see him.

daily.title: Hotel front desk
daily.description: A staff member speaks to a guest.
daily.example: If there's anything at all, please let us know.

work.title: Ending a business email
work.description: A modest line when attaching documents.
work.example: I hope this material will be of some help to you.

work.title: Charity event speech
work.description: Asking people to donate.
work.example: We would be grateful for any support, however small.

etymology: 「なり」 is a remnant of the classical copula 「なり」, and 「とも」 is a conjunctive particle for concessive conditions. Together they literally mean “even if it's ...”, which came to mean “even if only ...”.

similar.title: 〜たりとも
similar.explanation: Similar in form and often compared. 「〜たりとも」 attaches to 「一＋counter」 and is followed by a negative, meaning “not even one ...” (「一日たりとも休まない」); 「〜なりとも」 attaches to a word for a small amount and is followed by a wish, meaning “even a little would be fine”.

similar.title: 〜でも（question word + でも）
similar.explanation: 「何でも」 and 「どこでも」 mean the same as 「何なりと」 and 「どこへなりとも」 and are built the same way (copula + concessive). 「〜なりと」 is more formal and is often used in service language.

similar.title: 〜なり〜なり
similar.explanation: Same origin (the 「なり」 is the classical copula in both). 「〜なり〜なり」 lists options and means “either ... or ...” (「電話なりメールなりで」); 「〜なりとも」 expresses a wish for the bare minimum.

similar.title: 〜ないまでも
similar.explanation: Both contain the idea of “at least”. 「〜ないまでも」 means “even if not A, at least B”, setting two degrees against each other; 「〜なりとも」 gives only the bare minimum.

formation: It is built from the classical copula 「なり」 (equal to 「だ・である」) and the concessive conjunctive particle 「とも」 (equal to 「ても」), literally “even if it is ...”. Putting a word for a small amount into it (「少しなりとも」) gives “even if only a tiny bit (it's fine)”, expressing a wish to achieve something even at the minimum level. After a question word (「何なりと」) it means “anything at all (is fine)”, built the same way as 「何でも」 (「でも」 is also “copula + concessive”). Its classical elements make it formal and literary.

meaning: Something isn't worth it or there's no need to react that way. Like “there's no need to ...”.
connection: Verb dictionary form + には当たらない

senses.label: No need to
senses.meaning: The situation isn't serious enough to call for that reaction. Like “there's no need to ...” or “it's not worth ...”. Often used to tell someone not to be surprised, worried, critical, etc. Usually with verbs of judgment or feeling.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + には当たらない (common: 驚く・悲観する・非難する・心配する・感心する)
examples: His win reflects his true ability; it's nothing to be surprised about.
There's no need to be pessimistic over one failure.
His decision was unavoidable; there's no reason to criticize him.

notes: Noun + 「には当たらない」 means “does not constitute, does not correspond to”: 「違法行為には当たらない」 is “does not constitute an illegal act”, not “there's no need to break the law”, a completely different meaning.
It is mostly preceded by verbs of emotional or evaluative reaction (「驚く」, 「嘆く」, 「責める」, 「悲観する」); with ordinary actions it is unnatural: ✕「食べるには当たらない」→ ○「食べる必要はない」.
It carries a judging tone of “this is nothing”. Saying 「驚くには当たりません」 to a superior or client can come across as self-important; to comfort someone, 「ご心配には及びません」 is more suitable.

daily.title: Comforting a friend
daily.description: A friend is worried their child did badly on a test.
daily.example: He's only in first grade. There's no need to worry.

daily.title: News commentary
daily.description: A commentator talks about rising prices.
daily.example: A price rise this small is nothing to make a fuss about.

work.title: Speaking at a meeting
work.description: A department head reassures staff anxious about falling sales.
work.example: This is just a temporary dip; there's no need to be pessimistic.

work.title: Newspaper editorial
work.description: An editorial assesses a policy's effect.
work.example: This result was within expectations and is hardly surprising.

etymology: 「当たる」 originally means “to hit, to strike”, and came to mean “to correspond to, to be appropriate”. 「〜には当たらない」 means “doesn't call for ...”, and so “not worth, no need”.

similar.title: 〜には及ばない
similar.explanation: Same structure and close in meaning. 「〜には及ばない」 mostly means “there's no need to go to the trouble of ...” and is often used to politely decline (「お越しいただくには及びません」); 「〜には当たらない」 mostly follows verbs of emotional reaction and judges that “it doesn't deserve that reaction”.

similar.title: 〜までもない・〜までもなく
similar.explanation: 「〜までもない」 means “the matter is so obvious that there's no need to do it specially” (「言うまでもない」); 「〜には当たらない」 means “the matter isn't serious (or is only natural), so it doesn't deserve that reaction”.

similar.title: 〜ことはない
similar.explanation: 「〜ことはない」 is common in speech and directly tells the other person there's no need to do something (「心配することはない」); 「〜には当たらない」 is more formal, with the tone of an objective judgment.

similar.title: 〜に当たる
similar.explanation: Same origin (both from 「当たる」). 「〜に当たる」 means “to correspond to, to fall on” (「今年は申年に当たる」); this pattern is a negative use derived from “to fit”, meaning “not worth it”.

formation: It is made of “dictionary form of a verb + 「に」” (marking the object), 「は」 (topic or contrast), and 「当たらない」. 「当たる」 originally means “to hit, to run into”, and extends to “to correspond to, to be equivalent to”. 「驚くには当たらない」 literally says “for ‘being surprised’, (this matter) doesn't qualify or fit”, that is, “this isn't worth being surprised about”. So what it judges is not the action itself but whether the reaction fits the seriousness of the matter. That is why it is preceded by reaction verbs like 「驚く」, 「嘆く」 and 「責める」, and the second half implies that the matter is only natural.

meaning: Doing something ahead of others, other places, or another event; taking the lead.
connection: Noun + に先駆けて／に先駆け／に先駆けた + noun

senses.label: Ahead of
senses.meaning: Getting ahead of others of the same kind and doing something first. Like “ahead of ...” or “leading ...”. Usually a positive, pioneering act. Often after 「他社」, 「全国」, 「世界」, 「業界」.
senses.connection: Noun + に先駆けて (common: 他社・全国・世界・業界・他国)
examples: The company launched a new service ahead of its competitors.
This city was the first in the country to introduce fees for garbage collection.
Ahead of the public opening, a preview was held for the press.

senses.label: Leading, pioneering
senses.meaning: 「〜に先駆けた + noun」 modifies a noun: “pioneering ..., ahead of ...”. 「〜に先駆け、」 is a formal way to link clauses.
senses.connection: Noun + に先駆けた + noun; noun + に先駆け、〜
examples: This is a groundbreaking initiative, the first in the industry.
Japan put this technology into practical use ahead of the rest of the world.

notes: It stresses “leading ahead of others of the same kind, setting a precedent”; for a plain time order it is not used: ✕「会議に先駆けて資料を配る」→ ○「会議に先立って資料を配る」.
It carries the positive sense of “taking the lead, being a pioneer”, and is unnatural with bad things: ✕「全国に先駆けて事故が起きた」→ ○「全国で最初に事故が起きた」.
「先駆け」 is read 「さきがけ」, not 「せんく」; only 「先駆者」 is read 「せんくしゃ」.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: The news introduces a new product launch.
daily.example: The new smartphone will go on sale in Japan before overseas.

daily.title: Talking about your hometown

etymology: 「先駆け」 (さきがけ) originally meant being the first to charge into the enemy lines, from 「先に駆ける」. It came to mean “taking the lead, pioneer”, so 「〜に先駆けて」 means “charging out in front of ...”.

similar.title: 〜に先立って
similar.explanation: The one most often compared. 「〜に先立って」 means “before ... (doing preparations first)” and stresses time order (「開会に先立って挨拶する」); 「〜に先駆けて」 stresses being ahead of others of the same kind, with a pioneering sense.

similar.title: 〜を皮切りに
similar.explanation: Both relate to “being first”. 「〜を皮切りに」 means starting with something, after which a series of things happen one after another (「東京を皮切りに全国で公演する」); 「〜に先駆けて」 only stresses getting ahead of others.

similar.title: 〜まえに
similar.explanation: 「〜前に」 is the plainest “before ...” and shows only time order; 「〜に先駆けて」 is formal and carries the positive sense of getting ahead of others.

formation: 「先駆ける」 is made of 「先」 (front) and 「駆ける」 (to run), originally meaning to be the first to charge into the enemy line on horseback. The 「に」 in front marks the one who is outrun, so 「Aに先駆けて」 means “dashing out ahead of A”. It therefore expresses not only being early in time but also “being the first to open the way, setting a precedent”, and it often goes with new technologies, systems and products, with a positive tone. 「に先駆けた＋名詞」 uses the attributive form to modify a noun: “... that is ahead of ...”.

meaning: Judging something against a standard, such as laws, rules, or experience.
connection: Noun + に照らして／に照らし／に照らせば

senses.label: In light of a standard
senses.meaning: Uses laws, rules, common sense, etc. as a yardstick and makes a judgment. Like “in light of ...” or “according to ...”. Mostly for formal judgments and decisions.
senses.connection: Noun + に照らして／に照らし (common: 法律・規則・社会通念・基準・常識)
examples: Judged in light of the law, what he did is illegal.
The disciplinary action was decided in accordance with company rules.
By common social standards, that demand is unreasonable.

senses.label: Checking against experience or facts
senses.meaning: Uses past experience, facts, or records as a reference to infer or check. 「〜に照らせば」 and 「〜に照らすと」 mean “judging by ...”. 「照らし合わせる」 means “to cross-check”.
senses.connection: Noun + に照らせば／に照らすと; 〜を〜に照らし合わせる
examples: Judging by past experience, this plan should succeed.
Check the invoice against the purchase order.

notes: What comes before is a “standard” used for measuring (law, rules, common sense, experience), not material that you base your work on: ✕「データに照らして資料を作る」→ ○「データに基づいて資料を作る」.
「照らし合わせる」 is “to check, to compare”, while 「照らす」 alone is “to illuminate” (「ライトで足元を照らす」); keep them apart when reading.
Used to evaluate other people, it is heavy: 「常識に照らしてありえない」 is like saying the person has no common sense. Avoid it with clients and superiors; say 「一般的には難しいかと存じます」 instead.

etymology: 「照らす」 originally means “to shine light on”. It came to mean holding something up to the light to compare it, so 「〜に照らして」 means “looking at it in the light of ...”, measuring by a standard.

similar.title: 〜に基づいて
similar.explanation: 「〜に基づいて」 means doing something with data or facts as the basis (「データに基づいて作成する」); 「〜に照らして」 means measuring against a standard to judge whether something is appropriate.

similar.title: 〜に即して
similar.explanation: 「〜に即して」 means acting in close accordance with actual conditions or rules (「現状に即して対応する」); 「〜に照らして」 stresses making a judgment after comparing.

similar.title: 〜にのっとって
similar.explanation: 「〜にのっとって」 means doing something in line with rules, tradition or procedure (「伝統にのっとって式を行う」); 「〜に照らして」 means judging with the rules as the yardstick.

formation: 「照らす」 originally means “to shine light on”, and by extension “to hold things up in the light and compare them”. With 「に」 marking the standard of comparison, 「Aに照らして」 means “to shine the light of A on it” and see whether the thing matches A. So A must be something that can serve as a “ruler”, such as law, rules, common sense or experience, and the second half gives the judgment or handling reached after the comparison. 「照らし合わせる」 means to hold two things up against each other, that is, “to check”.
